newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka rebels say no plans for peace talks.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka rebels say no plans for peace talks.

text.p: Sri Lanka's Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) rebels, fighting a protracted war for an independent homeland, said on Wednesday there were no plans for peace talks with the government.
"There are no preparations for talks between the government and the LTTE at all," LTTE spokesman Anton Rajah said from London.

Rajah was reacting to local media speculation about peace talks following last week's agreement between the ruling People's Alliance coalition and the main opposition United National Party (UNP) to take a common approach to resolve the ethnic crisis.

President Chandrika Kumaratunga and UNP leader Ranil Wickremesinghe agreed that the party in opposition would not undermine any discussions between the majority party and any other group, including the LTTE, aimed at ending the conflict.

"We are aware that the government and the opposition have agreed in principle to a common approach to the national conflict, but it does not mean that they have agreed on any specific political plan," Rajah said.
"We have to wait and see whether the two parties will stick to their agreement," he added.
Sri Lankan Foreign Minister Lakshman Kadirgamar denied the rumours of peace talks last week, saying there was no plan at this point in time for negotiations with the LTTE.
Rajah said the LTTE would insist on international mediation in any possible talks.

"Since every successive Sri Lankan government had betrayed the Tamil people, the LTTE has insisted on international mediation should the possibility of talks arise," Rajah told Reuters over telephone.
The Sri Lankan government has in the past declined third party mediation to end the conflict, saying it was the island's internal matter.
The LTTE are fighting a 13-year-old war for an independent homeland for minority Tamils in Sinhalese majority Sri Lanka's north and east.
The government says more than 50,000 people have been killed in the war. The LTTE says the number is higher.
Rajah said any political negotiations must be preceded by conditions such as the withdrawal of troops from areas earlier held by the LTTE.

"The Chandrika government has said that the LTTE should lay down a substantial amount of arms as a precondition for talks. The LTTE's position is that it is not prepared to accept any such preconditons under any circumstances," Rajah said.
Peace talks between the government and the LTTE broke down in 1995 after the rebels sank two naval boats in the eastern Trincomalee harbour.
